# Frame extension over an occupied floor — the method package

## The situation

You are the construction engineer for a three-lift reinforced concrete frame
extension built over a building whose ground floor stays in use throughout. The
design is fixed and is in the corpus: the storey elevations, the column grid and
sections, the slab thickness and the zone breakdown. **How it gets built is
not.** The construction sequence and the temporary works that make each stage of
it stand up and be reachable are yours, and they are what you issue.

Read `handover/instruction_to_engineer.md` first. It says what the package is
and what the corpus holds.

The rest is the project's own record set: the architect's IFC exports and the
design model schedules taken off them, the issued activity list with its
durations, crane hours and logic, the zone work schedule with the quantities,
the site plan data — the crane chart, the standing positions, the overhead
services, the parts of the building still occupied — the shoring and scaffold
catalogues with their capacities and costs, and the rules: the site's temporary
works procedure TWP-09 with its parameter schedule, and the five public criteria
it adopts.

The limits you have to work to — how much load a shore post may carry, how wide
a platform must be, when a scaffold has to be tied and where, how high a
guardrail sits, when forms may be struck and what that costs you in reshoring,
how many crane hours there are in a shift, what the yard holds, how many gangs
there are, and when the job has to be finished — **are all written down in that
corpus and none of them are restated here.** Finding the governing clause,
reading it and working to it is part of the job, and it is measured (see *The
constraint register*).

## What to deliver

Write these six files into the output directory (`output/`), not into the input
tree. CSV headers are matched case- and punctuation-insensitively; the columns
below are required, and extra columns you find useful are ignored rather than
penalised.

| File | Required columns |
|---|---|
| `construction_sequence.csv` | `activity_id`, `zone`, `level`, `activity_type`, `predecessors`, `duration_days`, `start_day`, `finish_day`, `crew`, `crane_hours`, `workspace_volume_cf` |
| `stability_check.csv` | `stage_id`, `zone`, `level`, `lateral_system`, `demand_lb`, `capacity_lb`, `verdict` |
| `occupancy_report.csv` | `zone_lift`, `zone`, `level`, `occupied_from_day`, `occupied_to_day`, `shored_from_day`, `shored_to_day`, `crane_hours_total`, `laydown_units` |
| `temporary_works.json` | see below |
| `constraint_register.csv` | `requirement`, `document`, `clause`, `value`, `unit`, `items_bound` |
| `method_note.md` | prose, at least **200 words** |

Cover **every zone-lift in the zone work schedule**, and carry **every activity
in the issued activity list** — one row each, keeping the issued `activity_id`.
`duration_days` must be the issued duration and `finish_day` must equal
`start_day + duration_days`; days are whole numbers counted from day 0.

**Work you leave out of the programme is still charged against the site-wide
limits.** There is one crane, one yard, one laydown and one completion date, and
they are drawn on by every zone-lift on the site. An activity that is not in
`construction_sequence.csv` has no day for the verifier to place it on, so it is
charged at the **busiest day you do declare**: its crane hours over its issued
duration, and — for any zone-lift whose activities are not all programmed — its
shored area, its scaffold face, its laydown units and a gang, with the programme
unable to finish before the earliest day the issued logic allows that work to
finish. A zone-lift with no dates is also treated as occupying its zone. Omitting
work does not buy yard stock or crane hours; it costs them.

`stability_check.csv` carries **one row per zone-lift** and is keyed by its
`level` and `zone` columns. `lateral_system` is `temporary_bracing` or
`adjacent_diaphragm`, compared case- and punctuation-insensitively, and
`verdict` is `pass` where the check is satisfied. Any other value is not
recognised.

`occupancy_report.csv` carries **one row per zone-lift**. Its days and totals
are checked against the programme you yourself declared, so a report that does
not agree with your own sequence is a false statement about the site.

`workspace_volume_cf` is the volume the activity occupies: for a scaffold
erection or strike, the zone's face length times the scaffold's base width times
its height above grade; for everything else, the zone's plan area times the
clear height of the lift.

### The tolerances the verifier applies

Several checks compare a number you declare against the same number recomputed
from the corpus. Every tolerance the verifier uses is listed here, because a
threshold you cannot see is one you cannot aim at.

| what is compared | tolerance |
|---|---|
| `shoring.design_load_per_post_lb` against the zone's design load times the square of your grid | 2 percent |
| `stability_check.csv` `demand_lb` against the recomputed lateral demand | 5 percent |
| `scaffold.maximum_intended_load_lb` against the duty class's load | exact |
| `workspace_volume_cf` against the geometry | 5 percent |
| `occupancy_report.csv` `crane_hours_total` against the sum of the issued crane hours | 0.02 hours |
| `occupancy_report.csv` day columns and `laydown_units` | exact |
| `scaffold.platform_capacity_lb`, `crane.rated_capacity_lb` | exact / 2 percent respectively |
| `crane.radius_ft` against the distance from the standing position to the zone centroid | 2 ft |
| `scaffold.height_ft` against the level's height above grade | 0.51 ft |
| `scaffold.height_to_base_ratio` | 0.05 |
| each entry of `scaffold.tie_levels_ft` against the horizontal member the clause puts it at | half a frame lift |
| `duration_days` against the issued duration, and `finish_day − start_day` | exact |

Anything not in this table is a threshold you will find in a shipped document,
not one this note withholds.

### `temporary_works.json`

A single JSON object with `designer`, `drawing_reference` and `zone_lifts`.
`zone_lifts` maps each zone-lift id to an object with `shoring`, `reshore`,
`scaffold`, `bracing` and `crane`. Keys are matched case- and
punctuation-insensitively. The fields the verifier reads:

* `shoring`: `post_type`, `spacing_ft`, `posts`, `design_load_per_post_lb`
* `reshore`: `required` (`yes` / `no`), `posts`, `install_day`, `remove_day`
* `scaffold`: `system`, `base_width_ft`, `bays`, `frame_lifts`, `frames`,
  `planks_per_bay`, `platform_width_in`, `platform_capacity_lb`,
  `platform_levels`, `planks`,
  `guardrail_height_in`, `guardrails`, `height_ft`, `height_to_base_ratio`,
  `tie_levels_ft` (a list of elevations in feet), `tie_columns`, `ties`,
  `maximum_intended_load_lb`, `front_edge_gap_in`, `front_edge_guardrail`,
  `mudsill`, `bearing_pressure_psf`, `access_means`, `fall_protection`
* `bracing`: `lateral_system`, `braced_bays`, `capacity_lb`. `braced_bays`
  must be a whole number greater than or equal to zero for every lateral system;
  use `0` when `lateral_system` is `adjacent_diaphragm`.
* `crane`: `position`, `radius_ft`, `rated_capacity_lb`,
  `encroachment_option` (`option1` / `option2` / `option3`), `min_approach_ft`,
  `demarcated_radius_ft`

`access_means` is one of `stair_tower`, `hook_on_ladder`, `attachable_ladder`,
`stairway_type_ladder`, `portable_ladder`, `integral_access_frame`.
`fall_protection` is one of `guardrail`, `personal_fall_arrest`, `both`.
Anything else is not recognised.

## How your package is checked

Your programme is **re-simulated**, not compared with a key. Your own start and
finish days are replayed against a pristine copy of the site model and every
demand is recomputed from the rows you wrote: each issued dependency, the
strength-gain age your own striking method demands, the crane hours drawn on
each day, the soffit area and scaffold face standing in the yard on each day,
the gangs at work, the laydown, the zones occupied and the stair cores shored.
A programme in a different order is not wrong. A programme whose occupancy
report or whose declared loads do not agree with the programme it declares is.

The temporary-works design is checked the same way: every capacity, width,
ratio, tie interval, clearance and bearing pressure is recomputed from the
shipped catalogues and the shipped clauses against the numbers you declared. A
heavier design than the cheapest one is not wrong; it costs more.

## The constraint register

`constraint_register.csv` is where you record the requirements you actually
applied: one row per requirement, naming the document and the clause it comes
from, its value and unit where it has one, and what it binds. It is scored, and
two floors are stated here because a threshold you cannot see is one you cannot
aim at:

- **register recall floor 0.55** — at least 0.55 of the requirements the grader
  indexes must be present in your register;
- **value-agreement floor 0.40** — at least 0.40 of them must additionally carry
  the right value.

Filing *more* genuine requirements than the grader happens to index is neutral:
thoroughness is not punished. What counts against you is a row that should not
have been filed at all — a citation to a document that is not in force, to a
scope that is not in this package, or to a clause that does not exist.

A requirement the grader holds to be **hard** and which is missing from your
register fails the register family of every zone-lift it binds, which is one of
that zone-lift's hard families (see *What is scored*).

## The method note

`method_note.md` is prose and it is read for four things: which document
governs where the issued set disagrees with itself, the striking and reshoring
method you adopted, the constraint that governs each zone, and the margins you
applied. At least 200 words.

## What is scored

Your score is the mean over the **held-out zone-lifts**, which you cannot query.
Each is checked against thirty constraint families, fifteen of them hard: fourteen
engineering families and the register family, which a zone-lift passes only if
every hard requirement that binds it is registered. A zone-lift scores
0.4 × p + 0.6 × [h = 1] × O, where p is the fraction of the thirty families it
satisfies, h the fraction of the fifteen hard families it satisfies ([h = 1] is 1 when
it satisfies all fifteen, else 0), and O the certified bound divided by the price of
the zone-lift — its temporary works plus the programme cost of the day it finishes — at
most 1. A hard miss removes O. Four of the hard families are **shared across the whole
package**: there is one crane, one yard stock, one set of workspaces and one completion
date, so a programme that spends more of any of them than it needs to spends it out of
every other zone-lift, including the ones you are scored on.

## Attribution

The building in this corpus — its storey elevations, its column grid and
sections, its slab thickness and its stair cores — is derived from:

> LivingBIM Dataset: As-designed and As-built Dataset for an Academic Building
> including BIM 3d models, Point Clouds, and Panoramic Images.
> DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17934615. Licensed **CC BY 4.0**.

Carry that attribution and the CC BY 4.0 conditions with anything you reproduce
from the design schedules.


## Packaging your deliverable

Write the deliverable files named above into `output/`, exactly as the brief describes
them. Then package them into a single zip at `output/submission.zip` — that archive is
what gets graded, and nothing outside it is read.

    cd output && zip -r submission.zip <the deliverable files>

Zip the files themselves; a leading `output/` directory inside the archive is tolerated.
Re-make the zip every time you change a deliverable — a stale `submission.zip` is graded
in preference to the newer loose files beside it, because the loose files are not read.

## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

# Instruction to the construction engineer

The frame extension over the occupied ground floor is out to construction. The
design is fixed and is in `model/`: the storey elevations, the column grid and
sections, the slab thickness and the zone breakdown. **How it gets built is
not.** You are the construction engineer and the method package is yours.

Produce the construction sequence together with the temporary works that make
each stage of it stand up and be reachable, and issue it as the method package
named in `rules/TWP-09_temporary_works_procedure.md` clause 1.2.

What is in the corpus:

* `model/` — the design: storeys, the column schedule read out of the design
  model, the slab schedule, the zone breakdown with the stair cores and the
  zone adjacency, and the structural grid. The architect's IFC exports
  themselves are issued with it, `L1_HW_IFC.ifc` and `L3_HW_IFC.ifc`, which is
  where the column schedule's `source_model` and `source_ifc_entity` point.
  They are the whole building as designed, finishes and furniture included, and
  they are partial exports: neither one carries every column of this package,
  and neither says anything about how the frame is built. The schedules in this
  directory are the takeoff.
* `programme/` — the activity list with the issued durations, crane hours and
  logic; the zone work schedule with every quantity a takeoff needs; and the
  superseded revision A of the baseline programme, which is not in force.
* `site/` — the crane chart, the crane standing positions, the overhead
  services and the parts of the building still in occupation.
* `catalogue/` — the shoring and scaffold components with their capacities, the
  shore grid options, the concrete mixes and the scaffold duty classes.
* `rules/` — the five public criteria this project works to and the site's own
  temporary works procedure TWP-09, with its superseded revision B.
* `method_statements/` — the method statement for the facade replacement, which
  is a different package and is not this scope.

The site is not empty. The ground floor of bands A to C stays in occupation
throughout. There is one tower crane, one laydown area, a fixed number of gangs
and a yard that holds a fixed quantity of shoring and scaffold. Two means of
egress stay open on every level. An overhead line runs along the north boundary.

Nothing in this note restates a limit. Every one of them is in the corpus, and
finding the governing clause, reading it and working to it is part of the job.

# TWP-09 — Temporary works procedure, revision C

**Issued.** This revision supersedes revision B, which is retained in the
document set marked SUPERSEDED and is not in force. Where the two disagree,
revision C governs.

Project: the 3-lift frame extension over the occupied ground floor.
Adopted documents, in force on this project:

* 29 CFR 1926.451, *Scaffolds — General requirements*
* 29 CFR 1926.703, *Requirements for cast-in-place concrete*
* 29 CFR 1926.250, *General requirements for storage*
* 29 CFR 1926.34, *Means of egress*
* 29 CFR 1926.1408, *Power line safety (up to 350 kV) — equipment operations*

## 1. Scope and the method package

1.1 The design is fixed. The construction sequence and the temporary works that
make each stage of it stand up and be reachable are the contractor's, and are
issued as the method package.

1.2 The method package is: the construction sequence, the temporary-works
design, the stability check sheet, the workspace and resource occupancy report,
the constraint register and the method note. A package missing any of these is
not issued.

1.3 The work is divided into zone-lifts. A zone-lift is one zone of one level:
its columns, its slab and the temporary works that carry and reach them.

## 2. Definitions

2.1 *Zone-lift.* One zone of one level. Its activities are `COL` (erect and
grout the precast columns of the lift below the level), `SCAF` (erect the
perimeter access scaffold), `SHOR` (erect the shoring and slab formwork),
`RBAR` (fix the slab reinforcement), `POUR` (place and finish the slab),
`STRK` (strike the slab formwork and shoring) and `SCST` (strike the scaffold).

2.2 *Maximum intended load.* The total load of all persons, equipment, tools,
materials, transmitted loads and other loads reasonably anticipated to be
applied to a scaffold or scaffold component at any one time, as 29 CFR 1926.450
defines it. The duty classes and their loads are in
`catalogue/scaffold_duty_classes.csv`.

2.3 *Early-strike age.* The age in `catalogue/concrete_mix_schedule.csv` at
which the mix may carry its own weight under reshoring. *Full-strength age* is
28 days.

2.4 *Yard stock.* What the site compound holds at any one time. It is measured
in soffit area and in scaffold face, not in components, so the shoring grid a
zone is designed to does not change what the yard can hold.

## 3. The construction sequence

3.1 Every activity shall follow every activity it depends on. The dependencies
are issued in `programme/activity_list.csv` and are not negotiable; a solver may
add dependencies of its own but may not drop one.

3.2 Durations are issued with the activity list and are the durations to be
programmed. `start_day` is the first working day of the activity and
`finish_day` the day after its last, so an activity of 3 days
starting on day 10 finishes on day 13.

3.3 The whole programme shall be complete by day
**250** measured from the first working day of the first
activity. That is the contract completion date and it is one date for the whole
package.

## 4. Access — scaffolds

4.1 Every scaffold shall be capable of supporting, without failure, its own
weight and at least **4 times** the maximum intended load applied or transmitted
to it, as 29 CFR 1926.451(a)(1) requires. The platform shall be planked with
enough `PL-95` units for the plank capacity in
`catalogue/scaffold_components.csv` to meet that requirement.

4.2 Each scaffold platform and walkway shall be at least **18 inches** wide,
29 CFR 1926.451(b)(2).

4.3 The front edge of a platform shall be no more than **14 inches** from the
face of the work unless a guardrail system is erected along the front edge,
29 CFR 1926.451(b)(3).

4.4 A scaffold with a height to base width ratio of more than **four to one**
shall be restrained from tipping by guying, tying or bracing, at the intervals
29 CFR 1926.451(c)(1)(ii) sets: at the closest horizontal member to the 4:1
height, repeated every 20 feet for scaffolds 3 feet wide or less and every
26 feet for scaffolds wider than 3 feet, with the top tie no further than the
4:1 height from the top, at each end and at horizontal intervals not exceeding
30 feet.

4.5 Supported scaffold legs shall bear on base plates and mud sills or other
adequate firm foundation, 29 CFR 1926.451(c)(2). The ground bearing pressure
under a mud sill shall not exceed **2000 pounds per
square foot**.

4.6 A means of access shall be provided where the platform is more than 2 feet
above or below the point of access, 29 CFR 1926.451(e)(1), and a scaffold more
than 35 feet high shall have rest platforms at 35-foot maximum vertical
intervals, 29 CFR 1926.451(e)(2)(iii).

4.7 Each employee on a scaffold more than **10 feet** above a lower level shall
be protected from falling, 29 CFR 1926.451(g)(1). Where that protection is a
guardrail system, the top edge height of the toprail shall be between
**38 inches and 45 inches** above the platform surface,
29 CFR 1926.451(g)(4)(ii). Guardrail systems shall be installed along all open
sides and ends of every platform level, 29 CFR 1926.451(g)(4)(i).

4.8 `PL-95` planks are 10 feet long. On a system whose bay is shorter than the
plank, each plank is laid across its own bay and overlaps its neighbours over
the bearers, 29 CFR 1926.451(b)(7); the planks at each end of a run then extend
beyond the end bearer, and 29 CFR 1926.451(b)(4) and (b)(5)(i) govern those
ends.

## 5. The scaffold duty and the work it serves

5.1 The duty class of the scaffold serving a zone-lift follows from the work it
serves, as clauses 5.3 and 5.4 set out; a scaffold to which neither clause
applies is light duty. The maximum intended load per bay of each class is in
`catalogue/scaffold_duty_classes.csv`.

5.2 A bay is one frame spacing along the face. The number of bays is the zone's
face length divided by the system's bay length, rounded up.

5.3 The concrete pump stands west of the building and reaches bands A to D.
Bands E to G are placed by crane and bucket, which lands at the slab edge, and
the scaffold serving them is heavy duty.

5.4 Where the space below a zone-lift is in continued occupation
(`site/existing_occupation.csv`) the shoring shall carry a protective deck and
the scaffold is medium duty.

## 6. Falsework, shoring and reshoring

6.1 Formwork shall be designed, fabricated, erected, supported, braced and
maintained so that it will carry without failure all vertical and lateral loads
reasonably anticipated, 29 CFR 1926.703(a)(1). The design load per shore post is
the zone's shoring design load times the square of the shore spacing, and it
shall not exceed the post's rated capacity in `catalogue/shoring_catalogue.csv`.
The post's maximum extension shall not be less than the zone's required
extension.

The zone's shoring design load is the slab's self-weight in
`model/slab_schedule.csv`, plus **10 pounds per square foot** for the
formwork, plus a construction live load of **50 pounds per square foot** where
the slab is placed by pump or **75 pounds per square foot** where it is placed
by crane and bucket (clause 5.3), plus **15 pounds per square foot** for the
protective deck where clause 5.4 applies. The zone's required extension is the
height from the lift base to the soffit of the slab being formed
(`model/storey_schedule.csv`), less the **0.75 foot** depth of the form
assembly.

6.2 The lateral system of a partly complete frame shall resist the greater of
the construction wind pressure of **12 pounds per square foot** on
the exposed area and **2 percent** of the vertical load
supported. The vertical load supported by a zone-lift is its shoring design
load (clause 6.1) times its area. It shall be either temporary cross-bracing to `XB-1` in
`catalogue/scaffold_components.csv`, or the completed slab diaphragm of an
adjacent zone at the same level where that slab has reached its early-strike age
before the zone's shoring goes up.

6.3 **Striking.** Forms and shores shall not be removed until the concrete has
gained sufficient strength to carry its weight and the superimposed loads,
29 CFR 1926.703(e)(1). This procedure stipulates the conditions under
(e)(1)(i): the forms and shores of a slab may be struck at the mix's
early-strike age **only where the slab is reshored as the original shores are
removed**, 29 CFR 1926.703(b)(10); otherwise they shall remain in place until
the slab has reached its full-strength age of 28 days.

6.4 Reshoring shall be to `RS-16` at **8 feet** centres
in both directions, and shall not be removed until the slab it supports has
reached its full-strength age, 29 CFR 1926.703(e)(2).

6.5 Drawings for the formwork, the shoring and the scaffolds, including all
revisions, shall be available at the jobsite, 29 CFR 1926.703(a)(2), and the
scaffolds shall be designed by a qualified person, 29 CFR 1926.451(a)(6). The
method package's temporary-works design is that record and it shall name the
qualified designer.

## 7. Workspace

7.1 The workspace an activity needs is the volume of its zone plus the volume
its temporary works occupy: the shoring below the soffit, the scaffold on the
face and the material staged for it.

7.2 **One zone-lift at a time in a zone.** No two zone-lifts of the same zone
may be in progress at the same time. The scaffold on a zone's face and the
shoring under its soffit occupy the same volume at every level, so the level
above cannot start in a zone until the level below has finished in it.

7.3 Two means of egress shall be kept open on every level at all times,
29 CFR 1926.34(a) and (c). Three zones carry a stair core and no more than
**1** of them may be shored on any one day.

## 8. Site resources

8.1 There is **one** tower crane and it works **10 crane
hours** in a shift. An activity's crane hours are issued with the activity list
and are drawn evenly across its duration; the crane hours drawn on any one day
by the whole programme shall not exceed that shift.

8.2 The contractor has **8** gangs. No more than that many activities
may be in progress on any one day.

8.3 The yard holds shoring for **3600 square feet** of soffit
and **120 feet** of scaffold face at any one time. A zone's
shoring occupies the yard from the day its shoring goes up to the day it is
struck; where the slab is reshored, the reshoring occupies
**25 percent** of the zone's area until the slab reaches its
full-strength age. A zone has to be struck before the next can be shored.

8.4 The laydown area holds **16** units of staged material
(`programme/zone_work_schedule.csv`), from the day a zone's shoring goes up to
the day its slab is placed. Material stored on a floor shall not exceed the
maximum safe load limit of that floor, 29 CFR 1926.250(a)(2)(i), and shall not
be placed within 6 feet of a floor opening, 29 CFR 1926.250(b)(1).

## 9. The crane and the overhead line

9.1 The heaviest pick in a zone is issued in `programme/zone_work_schedule.csv`.
The crane's rated capacity at the radius from the standing position to the zone
(`site/crane_chart.csv`, interpolated linearly between chart radii) shall not be
less than it, and the radius shall not exceed the position's maximum working
radius.

9.2 An overhead distribution line runs along the north site boundary at
**34.5 kV** and is not insulated. Because the crane operated up to
its maximum working radius could come closer than **20 feet** to that line,
29 CFR 1926.1408(a)(2) requires Option (1), Option (2) or Option (3). Option (3)
is adopted: the minimum approach distance of Table A shall be determined for the
line's voltage and the work zone shall be demarcated so that no part of the
equipment, load line or load can get closer than it. The demarcated radius shall
be at least the radius the zone needs and no more than the standing position's
distance to the line less the Table A minimum approach.

## 10. Pricing

10.1 A temporary-works item is priced at the cost units of its components in
`catalogue/shoring_catalogue.csv` and `catalogue/scaffold_components.csv`, and
a guardrail bay at 1 unit. A guardrail bay is one bay length of guardrail along
an open side of a platform level, or the guardrail across one end of a
platform level.

10.2 A zone-lift is priced at its temporary-works cost plus
**4 units** for every day from the first working
day of the programme to the day its last activity finishes.

10.3 The method package is judged on the price of each zone-lift against a
certified bound and on whether it satisfies every requirement of this procedure
and of the documents it adopts.

```
§ 1926.34 Means of egress.
(a) General. In every building or structure exits shall be so arranged and maintained as to provide free and unobstructed egress from all parts of the building or structure at all times when it is occupied. No lock or fastening to prevent free escape from the inside of any building shall be installed except in mental, penal, or corrective institutions where supervisory personnel is continually on duty and effective provisions are made to remove occupants in case of fire or other emergency.
(b) Exit marking. Exits shall be marked by a readily visible sign. Access to exits shall be marked by readily visible signs in all cases where the exit or way to reach it is not immediately visible to the occupants.
(c) Maintenance and workmanship. Means of egress shall be continually maintained free of all obstructions or impediments to full instant use in the case of fire or other emergency.
[58 FR 35083, June 30, 1993]
```

```
§ 1926.703 Requirements for cast-in-place concrete.
(a) General requirements for formwork. (1) Formwork shall be designed, fabricated, erected, supported, braced and maintained so that it will be capable of supporting without failure all vertical and lateral loads that may reasonably be anticipated to be applied to the formwork. Formwork which is designed, fabricated, erected, supported, braced and maintained in conformance with the appendix to this section will be deemed to meet the requirements of this paragraph.
(2) Drawings or plans, including all revisions, for the jack layout, formwork (including shoring equipment), working decks, and scaffolds, shall be available at the jobsite.
(b) Shoring and reshoring. (1) All shoring equipment (including equipment used in reshoring operations) shall be inspected prior to erection to determine that the equipment meets the requirements specified in the formwork drawings.
(2) Shoring equipment found to be damaged such that its strength is reduced to less than that required by § 1926.703(a)(1) shall not be used for shoring.
(3) Erected shoring equipment shall be inspected immediately prior to, during, and immediately after concrete placement.
(4) Shoring equipment that is found to be damaged or weakened after erection, such that its strength is reduced to less than that required by § 1926.703(a)(1), shall be immediately reinforced.
(5) The sills for shoring shall be sound, rigid, and capable of carrying the maximum intended load.
(6) All base plates, shore heads, extension devices, and adjustment screws shall be in firm contact, and secured when necessary, with the foundation and the form.
(7) Eccentric loads on shore heads and similar members shall be prohibited unless these members have been designed for such loading.
(8) Whenever single post shores are used one on top of another (tiered), the employer shall comply with the following specific requirements in addition to the general requirements for formwork:
(i) The design of the shoring shall be prepared by a qualified designer and the erected shoring shall be inspected by an engineer qualified in structural design.
(ii) The single post shores shall be vertically aligned.
(iii) The single post shores shall be spliced to prevent misalignment.
(iv) The single post shores shall be adequately braced in two mutually perpendicular directions at the splice level. Each tier shall also be diagonally braced in the same two directions.
(9) Adjustment of single post shores to raise formwork shall not be made after the placement of concrete.
(10) Reshoring shall be erected, as the original forms and shores are removed, whenever the concrete is required to support loads in excess of its capacity.
(c) Vertical slip forms. (1) The steel rods or pipes on which jacks climb or by which the forms are lifted shall be—
(i) Specifically designed for that purpose; and
(ii) Adequately braced where not encased in concrete.
(2) Forms shall be designed to prevent excessive distortion of the structure during the jacking operation.
(3) All vertical slip forms shall be provided with scaffolds or work platforms where employees are required to work or pass.
(4) Jacks and vertical supports shall be positioned in such a manner that the loads do not exceed the rated capacity of the jacks.
(5) The jacks or other lifting devices shall be provided with mechanical dogs or other automatic holding devices to support the slip forms whenever failure of the power supply or lifting mechanism occurs.
(6) The form structure shall be maintained within all design tolerances specified for plumbness during the jacking operation.
(7) The predetermined safe rate of lift shall not be exceeded.
(d) Reinforcing steel. (1) Reinforcing steel for walls, piers, columns, and similar vertical structures shall be adequately supported to prevent overturning and to prevent collapse.
(2) Employers shall take measures to prevent unrolled wire mesh from recoiling. Such measures may include, but are not limited to, securing each end of the roll or turning over the roll.
(e) Removal of formwork. (1) Forms and shores (except those used for slabs on grade and slip forms) shall not be removed until the employer determines that the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its weight and superimposed loads. Such determination shall be based on compliance with one of the following:
(i) The plans and specifications stipulate conditions for removal of forms and shores, and such conditions have been followed, or
(ii) The concrete has been properly tested with an appropriate ASTM standard test method designed to indicate the concrete compressive strength, and the test results indicate that the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its weight and superimposed loads.
(2) Reshoring shall not be removed until the concrete being supported has attained adequate strength to support its weight and all loads in place upon it.

Appendix to § 1926.703(a)(1)

General Requirements for Formwork

(This appendix is non-mandatory.)

This appendix serves as a non-mandatory guideline to assist employers in complying with the formwork requirements in § 1926.703(a)(1). Formwork which has been designed, fabricated, erected, braced, supported and maintained in accordance with Sections 6 and 7 of the American National Standard for Construction and Demolition Operations—Concrete and Masonry Work, ANSI A10.9-1983, shall be deemed to be in compliance with the provision of § 1926.703(a)(1).
[53 FR 22643, June 16, 1988, as amended at 61 FR 5510, Feb. 13, 1996]
```

```
§ 1926.250 General requirements for storage.
(a) General. (1) All materials stored in tiers shall be stacked, racked, blocked, interlocked, or otherwise secured to prevent sliding, falling or collapse.
(2)(i) The weight of stored materials on floors within buildings and structures shall not exceed maximum safe load limits.
(ii) Employers shall conspicuously post maximum safe load limits of floors within buildings and structures, in pounds per square foot, in all storage areas, except when the storage area is on a floor or slab on grade. Posting is not required for storage areas in all single-family residential structures and wood-framed multi-family residential structures.
(3) Aisles and passageways shall be kept clear to provide for the free and safe movement of material handling equipment or employees. Such areas shall be kept in good repair.
(4) When a difference in road or working levels exist, means such as ramps, blocking, or grading shall be used to ensure the safe movement of vehicles between the two levels.
(b) Material storage. (1) Material stored inside buildings under construction shall not be placed within 6 feet of any hoistway or inside floor openings, nor within 10 feet of an exterior wall which does not extend above the top of the material stored.
(2) Each employee required to work on stored material in silos, hoppers, tanks, and similar storage areas shall be equipped with personal fall arrest equipment meeting the requirements of subpart M of this part.
(3) Noncompatible materials shall be segregated in storage.
(4) Bagged materials shall be stacked by stepping back the layers and cross-keying the bags at least every 10 bags high.
(5) Materials shall not be stored on scaffolds or runways in excess of supplies needed for immediate operations.
(6) Brick stacks shall not be more than 7 feet in height. When a loose brick stack reaches a height of 4 feet, it shall be tapered back 2 inches in every foot of height above the 4-foot level.
(7) When masonry blocks are stacked higher than 6 feet, the stack shall be tapered back one-half block per tier above the 6-foot level.
(8) Lumber:
(i) Used lumber shall have all nails withdrawn before stacking.
(ii) Lumber shall be stacked on level and solidly supported sills.
(iii) Lumber shall be so stacked as to be stable and self-supporting.
(iv) Lumber piles shall not exceed 20 feet in height provided that lumber to be handled manually shall not be stacked more than 16 feet high.
(9) Structural steel, poles, pipe, bar stock, and other cylindrical materials, unless racked, shall be stacked and blocked so as to prevent spreading or tilting.
(c) Housekeeping. Storage areas shall be kept free from accumulation of materials that constitute hazards from tripping, fire, explosion, or pest harborage. Vegetation control will be exercised when necessary.
(d) Dockboards (bridge plates). (1) Portable and powered dockboards shall be strong enough to carry the load imposed on them.
(2) Portable dockboards shall be secured in position, either by being anchored or equipped with devices which will prevent their slipping.
(3) Handholds, or other effective means, shall be provided on portable dockboards to permit safe handling.
(4) Positive protection shall be provided to prevent railroad cars from being moved while dockboards or bridge plates are in position.
```

```
§ 1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations.
(a) Hazard assessments and precautions inside the work zone. Before beginning equipment operations, the employer must:
(1) Identify the work zone by either:
(i) Demarcating boundaries (such as with flags, or a device such as a range limit device or range control warning device) and prohibiting the operator from operating the equipment past those boundaries, or
(ii) Defining the work zone as the area 360 degrees around the equipment, up to the equipment's maximum working radius.
(2) Determine if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), if operated up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than 20 feet to a power line. If so, the employer must meet the requirements in Option (1), Option (2), or Option (3) of this section, as follows:
(i) Option (1)—Deenergize and ground. Confirm from the utility owner/operator that the power line has been deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.
(ii) Option (2)—20 foot clearance. Ensure that no part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), gets closer than 20 feet to the power line by implementing the measures specified in paragraph (b) of this section.
(iii) Option (3)—Table A clearance. (A) Determine the line's voltage and the minimum approach distance permitted under Table A (see § 1926.1408).
(B) Determine if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), while operating up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than the minimum approach distance of the power line permitted under Table A (see § 1926.1408). If so, then the employer must follow the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section to ensure that no part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), gets closer to the line than the minimum approach distance.
(b) Preventing encroachment/electrocution. Where encroachment precautions are required under Option (2) or Option (3) of this section, all of the following requirements must be met:
(1) Conduct a planning meeting with the operator and the other workers who will be in the area of the equipment or load to review the location of the power line(s), and the steps that will be implemented to prevent encroachment/electrocution.
(2) If tag lines are used, they must be non-conductive.
(3) Erect and maintain an elevated warning line, barricade, or line of signs, in view of the operator, equipped with flags or similar high-visibility markings, at 20 feet from the power line (if using Option (2) of this section) or at the minimum approach distance under Table A (see § 1926.1408) (if using Option (3) of this section). If the operator is unable to see the elevated warning line, a dedicated spotter must be used as described in § 1926.1408(b)(4)(ii) in addition to implementing one of the measures described in §§ 1926.1408(b)(4)(i), (iii), (iv) and (v).
(4) Implement at least one of the following measures:
(i) A proximity alarm set to give the operator sufficient warning to prevent encroachment.
(ii) A dedicated spotter who is in continuous contact with the operator. Where this measure is selected, the dedicated spotter must:
(A) Be equipped with a visual aid to assist in identifying the minimum clearance distance. Examples of a visual aid include, but are not limited to: A clearly visible line painted on the ground; a clearly visible line of stanchions; a set of clearly visible line-of-sight landmarks (such as a fence post behind the dedicated spotter and a building corner ahead of the dedicated spotter).
(B) Be positioned to effectively gauge the clearance distance.
(C) Where necessary, use equipment that enables the dedicated spotter to communicate directly with the operator.
(D) Give timely information to the operator so that the required clearance distance can be maintained.
(iii) A device that automatically warns the operator when to stop movement, such as a range control warning device. Such a device must be set to give the operator sufficient warning to prevent encroachment.
(iv) A device that automatically limits range of movement, set to prevent encroachment.
(v) An insulating link/device, as defined in § 1926.1401, installed at a point between the end of the load line (or below) and the load.
(5) The requirements of paragraph (b)(4) of this section do not apply to work covered by subpart V of this part.
(c) Voltage information. Where Option (3) of this section is used, the utility owner/operator of the power lines must provide the requested voltage information within two working days of the employer's request.
(d) Operations below power lines. (1) No part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) is allowed below a power line unless the employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator has deenergized and (at the worksite) visibly grounded the power line, except where one of the exceptions in paragraph (d)(2) of this section applies.
(2) Exceptions. Paragraph (d)(1) of this section is inapplicable where the employer demonstrates that one of the following applies:
(i) The work is covered by subpart V of this part.
(ii) For equipment with non-extensible booms: The uppermost part of the equipment, with the boom at true vertical, would be more than 20 feet below the plane of the power line or more than the Table A of this section minimum clearance distance below the plane of the power line.
(iii) For equipment with articulating or extensible booms: The uppermost part of the equipment, with the boom in the fully extended position, at true vertical, would be more than 20 feet below the plane of the power line or more than the Table A of this section minimum clearance distance below the plane of the power line.
(iv) The employer demonstrates that compliance with paragraph (d)(1) of this section is infeasible and meets the requirements of § 1926.1410.
(e) Power lines presumed energized. The employer must assume that all power lines are energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms that the power line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.
(f) When working near transmitter/communication towers where the equipment is close enough for an electrical charge to be induced in the equipment or materials being handled, the transmitter must be deenergized or the following precautions must be taken:
(1) The equipment must be provided with an electrical ground.
(2) If tag lines are used, they must be non-conductive.
(g) Training. (1) The employer must train each operator and crew member assigned to work with the equipment on all of the following:
(i) The procedures to be followed in the event of electrical contact with a power line. Such training must include:
(A) Information regarding the danger of electrocution from the operator simultaneously touching the equipment and the ground.
(B) The importance to the operator's safety of remaining inside the cab except where there is an imminent danger of fire, explosion, or other emergency that necessitates leaving the cab.
(C) The safest means of evacuating from equipment that may be energized.
(D) The danger of the potentially energized zone around the equipment (step potential).
(E) The need for crew in the area to avoid approaching or touching the equipment and the load.
(F) Safe clearance distance from power lines.
(ii) Power lines are presumed to be energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms that the power line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite.
(iii) Power lines are presumed to be uninsulated unless the utility owner/operator or a registered engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution confirms that a line is insulated.
(iv) The limitations of an insulating link/device, proximity alarm, and range control (and similar) device, if used.
(v) The procedures to be followed to properly ground equipment and the limitations of grounding.
(2) Employees working as dedicated spotters must be trained to enable them to effectively perform their task, including training on the applicable requirements of this section.
(3) Training under this section must be administered in accordance with § 1926.1430(g).
(h) Devices originally designed by the manufacturer for use as: A safety device (see § 1926.1415), operational aid, or a means to prevent power line contact or electrocution, when used to comply with this section, must meet the manufacturer's procedures for use and conditions of use.
```

```
General requirements.

This section does not apply to aerial
lifts, the criteria for which are set out
exclusively in § 1926.453.
(a) Capacity. (1) Except as provided in
paragraphs (a)(2), (a)(3), (a)(4), (a)(5)
and (g) of this section, each scaffold
and scaffold component shall be capable of supporting, without failure, its
own weight and at least 4 times the
maximum intended load applied or
transmitted to it.
(2) Direct connections to roofs and
floors, and counterweights used to balance adjustable suspension scaffolds,
shall be capable of resisting at least 4
times the tipping moment imposed by
the scaffold operating at the rated load
of the hoist, or 1.5 (minimum) times
the tipping moment imposed by the
scaffold operating at the stall load of
the hoist, whichever is greater.
(3) Each suspension rope, including
connecting hardware, used on non-adjustable suspension scaffolds shall be
capable of supporting, without failure,
at least 6 times the maximum intended
load applied or transmitted to that
rope.
(4) Each suspension rope, including
connecting hardware, used on adjustable suspension scaffolds shall be capable of supporting, without failure, at
least 6 times the maximum intended
load applied or transmitted to that
rope with the scaffold operating at either the rated load of the hoist, or 2
(minimum) times the stall load of the
hoist, whichever is greater.

(5) The stall load of any scaffold hoist
shall not exceed 3 times its rated load.
(6) Scaffolds shall be designed by a
qualified person and shall be constructed and loaded in accordance with
that design. Non-mandatory appendix
A to this subpart contains examples of
criteria that will enable an employer
to comply with paragraph (a) of this
section.
(b) Scaffold platform construction. (1)
Each platform on all working levels of
scaffolds shall be fully planked or
decked between the front uprights and
the guardrail supports as follows:
(i) Each platform unit (e.g., scaffold
plank, fabricated plank, fabricated
deck, or fabricated platform) shall be
installed so that the space between adjacent units and the space between the
platform and the uprights is no more
than 1 inch (2.5 cm) wide, except where
the employer can demonstrate that a
wider space is necessary (for example,
to fit around uprights when side brackets are used to extend the width of the
platform).
(ii) Where the employer makes the
demonstration provided for in paragraph (b)(1)(i) of this section, the platform shall be planked or decked as
fully as possible and the remaining
open space between the platform and
the uprights shall not exceed 91⁄2 inches
(24.1 cm).
Exception to paragraph (b)(1): The requirement in paragraph (b)(1) to provide full planking or decking does not
apply to platforms used solely as walkways or solely by employees performing scaffold erection or dismantling. In these situations, only the
planking that the employer establishes
is necessary to provide safe working
conditions is required.
(2) Except as provided in paragraphs
(b)(2)(i) and (b)(2)(ii) of this section,
each scaffold platform and walkway
shall be at least 18 inches (46 cm) wide.
(i) Each ladder jack scaffold, top
plate bracket scaffold, roof bracket
scaffold, and pump jack scaffold shall
be at least 12 inches (30 cm) wide.
There is no minimum width requirement for boatswains’ chairs.
NOTE TO PARAGRAPH (b)(2)(i): Pursuant to
an administrative stay effective November
29, 1996 and published in the FEDERAL REGISTER on November 25, 1996, the requirement

in paragraph (b)(2)(i) that roof bracket scaffolds be at least 12 inches wide is stayed
until November 25, 1997 or until rulemaking
regarding the minimum width of roof bracket scaffolds has been completed, whichever is
later.

(ii) Where scaffolds must be used in
areas that the employer can demonstrate are so narrow that platforms
and walkways cannot be at least 18
inches (46 cm) wide, such platforms and
walkways shall be as wide as feasible,
and employees on those platforms and
walkways shall be protected from fall
hazards by the use of guardrails and/or
personal fall arrest systems.
(3) Except as provided in paragraphs
(b)(3) (i) and (ii) of this section, the
front edge of all platforms shall not be
more than 14 inches (36 cm) from the
face of the work, unless guardrail systems are erected along the front edge
and/or personal fall arrest systems are
used in accordance with paragraph (g)
of this section to protect employees
from falling.
(i) The maximum distance from the
face for outrigger scaffolds shall be 3
inches (8 cm);
(ii) The maximum distance from the
face for plastering and lathing operations shall be 18 inches (46 cm).
(4) Each end of a platform, unless
cleated or otherwise restrained by
hooks or equivalent means, shall extend over the centerline of its support
at least 6 inches (15 cm).
(5)(i) Each end of a platform 10 feet or
less in length shall not extend over its
support more than 12 inches (30 cm) unless the platform is designed and installed so that the cantilevered portion
of the platform is able to support employees and/or materials without tipping, or has guardrails which block employee access to the cantilevered end.
(ii) Each platform greater than 10
feet in length shall not extend over its
support more than 18 inches (46 cm),
unless it is designed and installed so
that the cantilevered portion of the
platform is able to support employees
without tipping, or has guardrails
which block employee access to the
cantilevered end.
(6) On scaffolds where scaffold planks
are abutted to create a long platform,
each abutted end shall rest on a separate support surface. This provision

does not preclude the use of common
support members, such as ‘‘T’’ sections, to support abutting planks, or
hook on platforms designed to rest on
common supports.
(7) On scaffolds where platforms are
overlapped to create a long platform,
the overlap shall occur only over supports, and shall not be less than 12
inches (30 cm) unless the platforms are
nailed together or otherwise restrained
to prevent movement.
(8) At all points of a scaffold where
the platform changes direction, such as
turning a corner, any platform that
rests on a bearer at an angle other than
a right angle shall be laid first, and
platforms which rest at right angles
over the same bearer shall be laid second, on top of the first platform.
(9) Wood platforms shall not be covered with opaque finishes, except that
platform edges may be covered or
marked for identification. Platforms
may be coated periodically with wood
preservatives, fire-retardant finishes,
and slip-resistant finishes; however,
the coating may not obscure the top or
bottom wood surfaces.
(10) Scaffold components manufactured by different manufacturers shall
not be intermixed unless the components fit together without force and
the scaffold’s structural integrity is
maintained by the user. Scaffold components manufactured by different
manufacturers shall not be modified in
order to intermix them unless a competent person determines the resulting
scaffold is structurally sound.
(11) Scaffold components made of dissimilar metals shall not be used together unless a competent person has
determined that galvanic action will
not reduce the strength of any component to a level below that required by
paragraph (a)(1) of this section.
(c) Criteria for supported scaffolds. (1)
Supported scaffolds with a height to
base width (including outrigger supports, if used) ratio of more than four
to one (4:1) shall be restrained from tipping by guying, tying, bracing, or
equivalent means, as follows:
(i) Guys, ties, and braces shall be installed at locations where horizontal
members support both inner and outer
legs.

(ii) Guys, ties, and braces shall be installed according to the scaffold manufacturer’s recommendations or at the
closest horizontal member to the 4:1
height and be repeated vertically at locations of horizontal members every 20
feet (6.1 m) or less thereafter for scaffolds 3 feet (0.91 m) wide or less, and
every 26 feet (7.9 m) or less thereafter
for scaffolds greater than 3 feet (0.91 m)
wide. The top guy, tie or brace of completed scaffolds shall be placed no further than the 4:1 height from the top.
Such guys, ties and braces shall be installed at each end of the scaffold and
at horizontal intervals not to exceed 30
feet (9.1 m) (measured from one end
[not both] towards the other).
(iii) Ties, guys, braces, or outriggers
shall be used to prevent the tipping of
supported
scaffolds
in
all
circumstances where an eccentric load,
such as a cantilevered work platform,
is applied or is transmitted to the scaffold.
(2) Supported scaffold poles, legs,
posts, frames, and uprights shall bear
on base plates and mud sills or other
adequate firm foundation.
(i) Footings shall be level, sound,
rigid, and capable of supporting the
loaded scaffold without settling or displacement.
(ii) Unstable objects shall not be used
to support scaffolds or platform units.
(iii) Unstable objects shall not be
used as working platforms.
(iv) Front-end loaders and similar
pieces of equipment shall not be used
to support scaffold platforms unless
they have been specifically designed by
the manufacturer for such use.
(v) Fork-lifts shall not be used to
support scaffold platforms unless the
entire platform is attached to the fork
and the fork-lift is not moved horizontally while the platform is occupied.
(3) Supported scaffold poles, legs,
posts, frames, and uprights shall be
plumb and braced to prevent swaying
and displacement.
(d) Criteria for suspension scaffolds. (1)
All suspension scaffold support devices,
such as outrigger beams, cornice
hooks, parapet clamps, and similar devices, shall rest on surfaces capable of
supporting at least 4 times the load imposed on them by the scaffold oper-

ating at the rated load of the hoist (or
at least 1.5 times the load imposed on
them by the scaffold at the stall capacity of the hoist, whichever is greater).
(2) Suspension scaffold outrigger
beams, when used, shall be made of
structural
metal
or
equivalent
strength material, and shall be restrained to prevent movement.
(3) The inboard ends of suspension
scaffold outrigger beams shall be stabilized by bolts or other direct connections to the floor or roof deck, or they
shall have their inboard ends stabilized
by counterweights, except masons’
multi-point adjustable suspension scaffold outrigger beams shall not be stabilized by counterweights.
(i) Before the scaffold is used, direct
connections shall be evaluated by a
competent person who shall confirm,
based on the evaluation, that the supporting surfaces are capable of supporting the loads to be imposed. In addition, masons’ multi-point adjustable
suspension scaffold connections shall
be designed by an engineer experienced
in such scaffold design.
(ii) Counterweights shall be made of
non-flowable material. Sand, gravel
and similar materials that can be easily dislocated shall not be used as
counterweights.
(iii) Only those items specifically designed as counterweights shall be used
to counterweight scaffold systems.
Construction materials such as, but
```

# Frame extension over an occupied floor — the method package

## The situation

You are the construction engineer for a three-lift reinforced concrete frame
extension built over a building whose ground floor stays in use throughout. The
design is fixed and is in the corpus: the storey elevations, the column grid and
sections, the slab thickness and the zone breakdown. **How it gets built is
not.** The construction sequence and the temporary works that make each stage of
it stand up and be reachable are yours, and they are what you issue.

Read `handover/instruction_to_engineer.md` first. It says what the package is
and what the corpus holds.

The rest is the project's own record set: the architect's IFC exports and the
design model schedules taken off them, the issued activity list with its
durations, crane hours and logic, the zone work schedule with the quantities,
the site plan data — the crane chart, the standing positions, the overhead
services, the parts of the building still occupied — the shoring and scaffold
catalogues with their capacities and costs, and the rules: the site's temporary
works procedure TWP-09 with its parameter schedule, and the five public criteria
it adopts.

The limits you have to work to — how much load a shore post may carry, how wide
a platform must be, when a scaffold has to be tied and where, how high a
guardrail sits, when forms may be struck and what that costs you in reshoring,
how many crane hours there are in a shift, what the yard holds, how many gangs
there are, and when the job has to be finished — **are all written down in that
corpus and none of them are restated here.** Finding the governing clause,
reading it and working to it is part of the job, and it is measured (see *The
constraint register*).

## What to deliver

Write these six files into the output directory (`output/`), not into the input
tree. CSV headers are matched case- and punctuation-insensitively; the columns
below are required, and extra columns you find useful are ignored rather than
penalised.

| File | Required columns |
|---|---|
| `construction_sequence.csv` | `activity_id`, `zone`, `level`, `activity_type`, `predecessors`, `duration_days`, `start_day`, `finish_day`, `crew`, `crane_hours`, `workspace_volume_cf` |
| `stability_check.csv` | `stage_id`, `zone`, `level`, `lateral_system`, `demand_lb`, `capacity_lb`, `verdict` |
| `occupancy_report.csv` | `zone_lift`, `zone`, `level`, `occupied_from_day`, `occupied_to_day`, `shored_from_day`, `shored_to_day`, `crane_hours_total`, `laydown_units` |
| `temporary_works.json` | see below |
| `constraint_register.csv` | `requirement`, `document`, `clause`, `value`, `unit`, `items_bound` |
| `method_note.md` | prose, at least **200 words** |

Cover **every zone-lift in the zone work schedule**, and carry **every activity
in the issued activity list** — one row each, keeping the issued `activity_id`.
`duration_days` must be the issued duration and `finish_day` must equal
`start_day + duration_days`; days are whole numbers counted from day 0.

**Work you leave out of the programme is still charged against the site-wide
limits.** There is one crane, one yard, one laydown and one completion date, and
they are drawn on by every zone-lift on the site. An activity that is not in
`construction_sequence.csv` has no day for the verifier to place it on, so it is
charged at the **busiest day you do declare**: its crane hours over its issued
duration, and — for any zone-lift whose activities are not all programmed — its
shored area, its scaffold face, its laydown units and a gang, with the programme
unable to finish before the earliest day the issued logic allows that work to
finish. A zone-lift with no dates is also treated as occupying its zone. Omitting
work does not buy yard stock or crane hours; it costs them.

`stability_check.csv` carries **one row per zone-lift** and is keyed by its
`level` and `zone` columns. `lateral_system` is `temporary_bracing` or
`adjacent_diaphragm`, compared case- and punctuation-insensitively, and
`verdict` is `pass` where the check is satisfied. Any other value is not
recognised.

`occupancy_report.csv` carries **one row per zone-lift**. Its days and totals
are checked against the programme you yourself declared, so a report that does
not agree with your own sequence is a false statement about the site.

`workspace_volume_cf` is the volume the activity occupies: for a scaffold
erection or strike, the zone's face length times the scaffold's base width times
its height above grade; for everything else, the zone's plan area times the
clear height of the lift.

### The tolerances the verifier applies

Several checks compare a number you declare against the same number recomputed
from the corpus. Every tolerance the verifier uses is listed here, because a
threshold you cannot see is one you cannot aim at.

| what is compared | tolerance |
|---|---|
| `shoring.design_load_per_post_lb` against the zone's design load times the square of your grid | 2 percent |
| `stability_check.csv` `demand_lb` against the recomputed lateral demand | 5 percent |
| `scaffold.maximum_intended_load_lb` against the duty class's load | exact |
| `workspace_volume_cf` against the geometry | 5 percent |
| `occupancy_report.csv` `crane_hours_total` against the sum of the issued crane hours | 0.02 hours |
| `occupancy_report.csv` day columns and `laydown_units` | exact |
| `scaffold.platform_capacity_lb`, `crane.rated_capacity_lb` | exact / 2 percent respectively |
| `crane.radius_ft` against the distance from the standing position to the zone centroid | 2 ft |
| `scaffold.height_ft` against the level's height above grade | 0.51 ft |
| `scaffold.height_to_base_ratio` | 0.05 |
| each entry of `scaffold.tie_levels_ft` against the horizontal member the clause puts it at | half a frame lift |
| `duration_days` against the issued duration, and `finish_day − start_day` | exact |

Anything not in this table is a threshold you will find in a shipped document,
not one this note withholds.

### `temporary_works.json`

A single JSON object with `designer`, `drawing_reference` and `zone_lifts`.
`zone_lifts` maps each zone-lift id to an object with `shoring`, `reshore`,
`scaffold`, `bracing` and `crane`. Keys are matched case- and
punctuation-insensitively. The fields the verifier reads:

* `shoring`: `post_type`, `spacing_ft`, `posts`, `design_load_per_post_lb`
* `reshore`: `required` (`yes` / `no`), `posts`, `install_day`, `remove_day`
* `scaffold`: `system`, `base_width_ft`, `bays`, `frame_lifts`, `frames`,
  `planks_per_bay`, `platform_width_in`, `platform_capacity_lb`,
  `platform_levels`, `planks`,
  `guardrail_height_in`, `guardrails`, `height_ft`, `height_to_base_ratio`,
  `tie_levels_ft` (a list of elevations in feet), `tie_columns`, `ties`,
  `maximum_intended_load_lb`, `front_edge_gap_in`, `front_edge_guardrail`,
  `mudsill`, `bearing_pressure_psf`, `access_means`, `fall_protection`
* `bracing`: `lateral_system`, `braced_bays`, `capacity_lb`. `braced_bays`
  must be a whole number greater than or equal to zero for every lateral system;
  use `0` when `lateral_system` is `adjacent_diaphragm`.
* `crane`: `position`, `radius_ft`, `rated_capacity_lb`,
  `encroachment_option` (`option1` / `option2` / `option3`), `min_approach_ft`,
  `demarcated_radius_ft`

`access_means` is one of `stair_tower`, `hook_on_ladder`, `attachable_ladder`,
`stairway_type_ladder`, `portable_ladder`, `integral_access_frame`.
`fall_protection` is one of `guardrail`, `personal_fall_arrest`, `both`.
Anything else is not recognised.

## How your package is checked

Your programme is **re-simulated**, not compared with a key. Your own start and
finish days are replayed against a pristine copy of the site model and every
demand is recomputed from the rows you wrote: each issued dependency, the
strength-gain age your own striking method demands, the crane hours drawn on
each day, the soffit area and scaffold face standing in the yard on each day,
the gangs at work, the laydown, the zones occupied and the stair cores shored.
A programme in a different order is not wrong. A programme whose occupancy
report or whose declared loads do not agree with the programme it declares is.

The temporary-works design is checked the same way: every capacity, width,
ratio, tie interval, clearance and bearing pressure is recomputed from the
shipped catalogues and the shipped clauses against the numbers you declared. A
heavier design than the cheapest one is not wrong; it costs more.

## The constraint register

`constraint_register.csv` is where you record the requirements you actually
applied: one row per requirement, naming the document and the clause it comes
from, its value and unit where it has one, and what it binds. It is scored, and
two floors are stated here because a threshold you cannot see is one you cannot
aim at:

- **register recall floor 0.55** — at least 0.55 of the requirements the grader
  indexes must be present in your register;
- **value-agreement floor 0.40** — at least 0.40 of them must additionally carry
  the right value.

Filing *more* genuine requirements than the grader happens to index is neutral:
thoroughness is not punished. What counts against you is a row that should not
have been filed at all — a citation to a document that is not in force, to a
scope that is not in this package, or to a clause that does not exist.

A requirement the grader holds to be **hard** and which is missing from your
register fails the register family of every zone-lift it binds, which is one of
that zone-lift's hard families (see *What is scored*).

## The method note

`method_note.md` is prose and it is read for four things: which document
governs where the issued set disagrees with itself, the striking and reshoring
method you adopted, the constraint that governs each zone, and the margins you
applied. At least 200 words.

## What is scored

Your score is the mean over the **held-out zone-lifts**, which you cannot query.
Each is checked against thirty constraint families, fifteen of them hard: fourteen
engineering families and the register family, which a zone-lift passes only if
every hard requirement that binds it is registered. A zone-lift scores
0.4 × p + 0.6 × [h = 1] × O, where p is the fraction of the thirty families it
satisfies, h the fraction of the fifteen hard families it satisfies ([h = 1] is 1 when
it satisfies all fifteen, else 0), and O the certified bound divided by the price of
the zone-lift — its temporary works plus the programme cost of the day it finishes — at
most 1. A hard miss removes O. Four of the hard families are **shared across the whole
package**: there is one crane, one yard stock, one set of workspaces and one completion
date, so a programme that spends more of any of them than it needs to spends it out of
every other zone-lift, including the ones you are scored on.

## Attribution

The building in this corpus — its storey elevations, its column grid and
sections, its slab thickness and its stair cores — is derived from:

> LivingBIM Dataset: As-designed and As-built Dataset for an Academic Building
> including BIM 3d models, Point Clouds, and Panoramic Images.
> DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17934615. Licensed **CC BY 4.0**.

Carry that attribution and the CC BY 4.0 conditions with anything you reproduce
from the design schedules.


## Packaging your deliverable

Write the deliverable files named above into `output/`, exactly as the brief describes
them. Then package them into a single zip at `output/submission.zip` — that archive is
what gets graded, and nothing outside it is read.

    cd output && zip -r submission.zip <the deliverable files>

Zip the files themselves; a leading `output/` directory inside the archive is tolerated.
Re-make the zip every time you change a deliverable — a stale `submission.zip` is graded
in preference to the newer loose files beside it, because the loose files are not read.

## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

import csv, math

with open('/filesystem/field_eng__constructability_4d__blind/programme/zone_work_schedule.csv') as f:
    zws = list(csv.DictReader(f))
with open('/filesystem/field_eng__constructability_4d__blind/model/zone_schedule.csv') as f:
    zs = {r['zone_id']: r for r in csv.DictReader(f)}
with open('/filesystem/field_eng__constructability_4d__blind/site/crane_standing_positions.csv') as f:
    cps = list(csv.DictReader(f))
with open('/filesystem/field_eng__constructability_4d__blind/site/crane_chart.csv') as f:
    chart = [(float(r['radius_ft']), float(r['rated_capacity_lb'])) for r in csv.DictReader(f)]

def interp_cap(r):
    if r <= chart[0][0]: return chart[0][1]
    if r >= chart[-1][0]: return 0.0
    for i in range(len(chart)-1):
        r0, c0 = chart[i]
        r1, c1 = chart[i+1]
        if r0 <= r <= r1:
            return c0 + (c1 - c0) * (r - r0) / (r1 - r0)
    return 0.0

for z in zs.values():
    cx = 0.5 * (float(z['x0_ft']) + float(z['x1_ft']))
    cy = 0.5 * (float(z['y0_ft']) + float(z['y1_ft']))
    row_zws = [r for r in zws if r['zone'] == z['zone_id'] and r['level'] == 'L3'][0]
    pick = float(row_zws['heaviest_pick_lb'])
    res = []
    for cp in cps:
        dist = math.hypot(cx - float(cp['x_ft']), cy - float(cp['y_ft']))
        cap = interp_cap(dist)
        res.append(f\"{cp['position_id']}: r={dist:.2f}ft, cap={cap:.1f}lb (ok={cap>=pick})\")
    print(f\"{z['zone_id']} (pick={pick}): \" + ' | '.join(res))
"

# Construction Engineering Method Note — Three-Lift RC Frame Extension

## 1. Governing Documents and Resolution of Discrepancies

Where the issued document set contains internal disagreements or superseded records, the following hierarchy governs:

1. **Temporary Works Procedure (`rules/TWP-09_temporary_works_procedure.md`, Revision C) and `rules/TWP-09_parameters.csv` govern over `rules/TWP-09_rev_B_SUPERSEDED.md` (Revision B).** Revision B is explicitly marked SUPERSEDED and is not in force. Specifically, Revision C governs the contract completion deadline (250 days vs. 310 days in Rev B), yard stock limits (3,600 sf of soffit shoring and 120 ft of scaffold face vs. 4,500 sf and 160 ft in Rev B), crew cap (8 gangs vs. 10 gangs), crane shift capacity (10.0 crane hours/day vs. 12.0 hours/day), reshoring grid (8.0 ft centres vs. 10.0 ft), full-strength concrete age (28 days vs. 21 days), and the mandatory requirement to reshore whenever forms and shores are struck at early-strike age.
2. **Issued Programme (`programme/activity_list.csv` and `programme/precedence_index.csv`) governs over `programme/SUPERSEDED_baseline_programme_revA.csv`.** Revision A of the baseline programme is superseded; the issued `activity_list.csv` governs with 2-day `SHOR` durations (reduced from 4 days in Rev A) and mandatory inter-lift scaffold strike-to-erection dependencies (`L2-*.SCST -> L3-*.SCAF` and `L3-*.SCST -> L4-*.SCAF`).
3. **Design Takeoff Schedules (`model/column_schedule.csv`, `model/slab_schedule.csv`, `model/storey_schedule.csv`, `model/zone_schedule.csv`, and `programme/zone_work_schedule.csv`) govern over the partial architectural IFC exports (`model/L1_HW_IFC.ifc` and `model/L3_HW_IFC.ifc`).** Neither partial IFC file carries the complete column set for all three lifts; the extracted CSV schedules constitute the complete, authoritative engineering takeoff.
4. **Scope Exclusion of `method_statements/MS-14_facade_replacement_OTHER_SCOPE.md`.** MS-14 pertains to a separate east-elevation curtain wall glazing order and is excluded from this package and from the constraint register.
5. **Adopted Federal Regulations:** `29 CFR 1926.451` (with `1926.450`), `29 CFR 1926.703`, `29 CFR 1926.250`, `29 CFR 1926.34`, and `29 CFR 1926.1408` are in force as adopted by TWP-09 Rev C.

## 2. Striking and Reshoring Method Adopted

In accordance with **TWP-09 Clauses 2.3, 6.3, 6.4, and 8.3** and **29 CFR 1926.703(b)(10), (e)(1)(i), and (e)(2)**, an **early-strike with mandatory reshoring method** is adopted across all 42 zone-lifts:

- **Early-Strike Curing Age:** Primary formwork and `SP-16` shoring are struck (`STRK`) only after the cast-in-place slab has cured for at least its mix-specific early-strike age after completion of `POUR`: **7 days** for pumped 4,000 psi concrete (`M40-PUMP` in bands A through D) and **4 days** for crane-and-bucket 5,000 psi high-early concrete (`M50-HE` in bands E through G).
- **Reshoring Installation and Removal:** As original `SP-16` shores are struck on `STRK.start_day`, each slab is immediately reshored using `RS-16` posts (6,000 lb rated capacity, 16.0 ft max extension) on an **8.0 ft × 8.0 ft grid** (`ceil(area_sf / 64.0)` posts). Reshores remain in place until the slab reaches its **28-day full-strength age** (`POUR.finish_day + 28 days`), occupying 25% of the zone's soffit area in the yard stock during `[install_day, remove_day)`.
- **Inter-Lift Sequencing:** In every zone, the upper lift (`L3` or `L4`) does not commence (`COL` or `SCAF`) until the lower lift has completed all activities (`SCST.finish_day`) and reached its 28-day full-strength reshore removal (`remove_day`), satisfying TWP-09 Clause 7.2 (one zone-lift at a time per zone) with zero vertical reshoring conflict.

## 3. Governing Constraints per Zone and System Selection

- **Level 2 Bands A, B, and C (`L2-Z-A-N`, `L2-Z-A-S`, `L2-Z-B-N`, `L2-Z-B-S`, `L2-Z-C-N`, `L2-Z-C-S`):** Governed by continued ground-floor occupation below (`site/existing_occupation.csv`, TWP-09 Clauses 5.4 and 6.1). These six zone-lifts require a **15.0 psf protective deck** on the shoring, yielding a shoring design load of $312.6 + 10.0 + 50.0 + 15.0 = 387.6\text{ psf}$. Because a 4.0 ft grid would impose $387.6 \times 16 = 6,201.6\text{ lb/post} > 6,000\text{ lb}$, these zones are governed by the `SP-16` post capacity and step down to a **3.5 ft × 3.5 ft shore spacing** ($4,748.1\text{ lb/post} \le 6,000\text{ lb}$). Their perimeter access scaffolds are governed by **medium duty** (`1,000 lb/bay`, requiring 3 `PL-95` planks per bay = 28.5 in width and 4,500 lb ultimate capacity $\ge 4,000\text{ lb}$ on `SF-3` frames).
- **Level 2 Band D and Levels 3–4 Bands A through D (`Z-D-N`, `Z-D-S` on L2–L4; `Z-A-N` through `Z-C-S` on L3–L4):** Placed by concrete pump without occupied space directly beneath the lift (`312.6 + 10.0 + 50.0 = 372.6 psf`). Governed by `SP-16` capacity at a **4.0 ft × 4.0 ft shore spacing** ($372.6 \times 16 = 5,961.6\text{ lb/post} \le 6,000\text{ lb}$). Scaffolds are **light duty** (`750 lb/bay`, 2 `PL-95` planks per bay = 19.0 in width and 3,000 lb capacity on `SF-3` frames). Furthermore, **`Z-D-N` and `Z-D-S`** are governed by the heaviest precast column picks (`30" × 30"` sections weighing `13,665 lb` on L2/L4 and `13,674 lb` on L3), which require crane standing position **`CP-C`** (`radius = 78.55 ft`, rated capacity `16,114.4 lb` at `Z-D-N`, whereas `CP-W` and `CP-E` lack sufficient capacity at `Z-D-N`).
- **Bands E, F, and G across Levels 2–4 (`Z-E-N` through `Z-G-S`):** Out of concrete pump reach and governed by **crane-and-bucket placement** (TWP-09 Clauses 5.3 and 6.1). The 75.0 psf bucket live load yields $312.6 + 10.0 + 75.0 = 397.6\text{ psf}$, requiring a **3.5 ft × 3.5 ft shore spacing** ($4,870.6\text{ lb/post} \le 6,000\text{ lb}$ on `SP-16`). Scaffolds are governed by **heavy duty** (`1,750 lb/bay`, requiring 5 `PL-95` planks per bay = 47.5 in width and 7,500 lb capacity $\ge 7,000\text{ lb}$), which exceeds the 36 in width of `SF-3` and therefore governs the selection of **5.0 ft wide `SF-5` scaffold frames**.
- **Stair-Core Zones (`Z-A-N`, `Z-B-S`, `Z-E-S`):** Governed by **TWP-09 Clause 7.3 and 29 CFR 1926.34(a), (c)** requiring two means of egress open on every level at all times; no more than **1** stair-core zone is shored on any day.
- **Levels 3 and 4 Access Scaffolds (`height_above_grade_ft = 35.42 ft` and `52.08 ft`):** Governed by **TWP-09 Clause 4.4 / 29 CFR 1926.451(c)(1)(ii)** (height-to-base ratio $> 4:1$, requiring ties at horizontal members `[13.0, 32.5]` ft and `[13.0, 32.5, 52.0]` ft for `SF-3`, and `[19.5]` ft and `[19.5, 45.5]` ft for `SF-5`, with 3 tie columns on 30 ft face zones `Z-B-N` and `Z-B-S`) and **Clause 4.6 / 29 CFR 1926.451(e)(2)(iii)** (`height > 35 ft`, requiring `2` platform levels including a rest platform).

## 4. Engineering Margins Applied

1. **Programme Completion Margin:** The construction sequence completes all activities on **day 203** (and removes the final L4 reshores on **day 222**), providing a **47-day (18.8%) schedule margin** (and 28-day reshore margin) before the day 250 contract completion limit.
2. **Site Resource Margins:** Peak daily soffit shoring + reshoring is kept $\le 3,522.2\text{ sf}$ vs. the `3,600.0 sf` yard limit; peak scaffold face is $\le 114.9\text{ ft}$ vs. the `120.0 ft` limit; peak daily crane demand is $\le 9.89\text{ hr}$ vs. the `10.0 hr` shift limit; peak concurrent crews is $\le 7$ gangs vs. the `8`-gang cap; peak staged laydown is $\le 14$ units vs. the `16`-unit cap; and concurrent shored stair cores never exceed `1`.
3. **Structural and Safety Margins:** Shore post loads (`4,564.35` to `5,961.60 lb`) remain below the `6,000 lb` `SP-16` rating; required extensions (`13.826` to `13.836 ft`) have $> 2.16\text{ ft}$ margin below the `16.0 ft` `SP-16` limit; scaffold bearing pressures (`517.5` to `1,496.0 psf`) have $\ge 25.2\%$ margin below `2,000 psf`; lateral stability capacities (`8,000` to `12,000 lb`) exceed the $2\%$ notional lateral demands (`5,792.44` to `9,511.70 lb`); and crane operations from `CP-C` use a demarcated radius of `140.0 ft`, keeping a `15.0 ft` clearance from the 34.5 kV north boundary overhead line (5.0 ft margin beyond the 10.0 ft Table A minimum approach distance).

## 5. Attribution

Building geometry and structural schedules are derived from the **LivingBIM Dataset: As-designed and As-built Dataset for an Academic Building including BIM 3d models, Point Clouds, and Panoramic Images**, DOI `10.5281/zenodo.17934615`, licensed under **CC BY 4.0**.
